name: David Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, David. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at a gold mine, a 150-tonne truck, taking ore from the shovel up the ramp to the crusher. Seven days on, seven off, day shift and night shift. Before this I drove forklifts in a supermarket warehouse for nineteen years, until they put in automatic shelving robots and cut the night crew from forty people to six. That was four years ago, and I came here at fifty-five.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: So you've seen automation up close already.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have. And here's the funny thing: the mine's got self-driving trucks on the north pit already, a trial with twelve of them, while we drive the south pit by hand. I look across at them at lunch, no cab lights, just going round. I keep a little notebook of how many loads they do compared with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, the trucks on the north pit were the most it was ever going to be. I'd tell the guys at lunch the robots plateaued, like everything does. I might share a news story in the family chat, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but I wouldn't fully believe it. The north pit trucks are already here, AI hype or not. So even in a quiet picture, I'd keep one eye on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and try to move up from the south pit to the bigger trucks on the main ramp, which pay a bit more. I'd use the AI on my phone now and then, like I do to check my roster and my tax. And I'd keep saving about five hundred a month, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with one eye open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loads per shift, mostly. Last month, the robot trucks did about the same as our best driver, and better than me, to be honest. But they stop dead when it rains hard or a sensor gets mud on it, and then a guy has to drive out and wipe it with a rag. That's the part nobody puts in the brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI on your phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter put it on there. I ask it things like, explain this line on my payslip, or what's the difference between these two super funds. I check it with someone before I do anything, but it's quicker than waiting on hold.

S0.say: I'd say the north pit robot trucks were as far as it was ever going to go, and that AI plateaued like everything does. He might share a news story in the family chat.
S0.think: He'd be relieved but not fully convinced, because the self-driving trucks are already on site whatever happens with AI. He'd keep an eye on them.
S0.do: Keeps driving and aims to move up to the bigger trucks on the main ramp for better pay. Keeps using AI now and then for rosters and tax, and saves about five hundred a month.
S0.quote: They stop dead when it rains hard or a sensor gets mud on it, and then a guy has to drive out and wipe it with a rag.
S0.fieldNote: David has already lost a job to warehouse robots and now watches self-driving trucks across the pit. He keeps a notebook comparing them with human drivers, which is a striking habit. He uses AI casually and always checks it with a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the sensible middle. Companies should do it carefully and help people move, and workers shouldn't fight what's already coming. I'd say that at lunch, though some of the older guys would argue with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the south pit goes driverless within three or four years in this picture, and I'm the newest driver on it. I've seen this film already, in the warehouse. They don't fire you all at once; they just stop replacing people and move you to the worst shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch who gets moved where over the first six months. Once a couple of guys have gone through the company's training for the control room and it works out, I'd put my name down too. Meanwhile I'd look at the quarry thirty minutes away, which runs older trucks and won't automate soon, as a backup, and I'd move another hundred a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I know what's coming because I've lived it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to you in the warehouse that shapes this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They told us nothing would change, then the robots came in over one summer. I was on the night crew; they moved me to days, then cut my hours, then offered a payout. I took it and came here, but I swore I'd see it coming next time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show her the notebook and say, look, here's my plan A and plan B. She works in the front office at a primary school and she likes plans. She'd say, just don't wait as long as last time.

S1.say: I'd say it's the sensible middle: companies should go carefully and help people move, and workers shouldn't fight what's already coming. Some older drivers would argue with him.
S1.think: He thinks the south pit would go driverless within three or four years, and he's the newest driver. He's seen this before: they stop replacing people and move you to the worst shifts.
S1.do: Watches who gets moved in the first six months and joins the control room training once a few colleagues have succeeded. Keeps a nearby quarry with older trucks as a backup and saves an extra hundred a month.
S1.feel: Anxious, because he's lived through this before.
S1.quote: They don't fire you all at once; they just stop replacing people and move you to the worst shifts.
S1.fieldNote: His warehouse experience makes even steady change feel close and real. He waits for proof before acting, then plans carefully with a backup. Elena's line about not waiting as long as last time shows how the past shapes him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both the companies and the government need to slow down and look after people. I'm not a big politics person, but two years is too fast for anybody. I'd say it to my local member if she asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's over for me at the mine within a year. Robot trucks already work; with full AGI they'd fix the problems I wrote in my notebook too. And the quarry backup goes the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take whatever payout they offer early, before the money runs dry. I'd stop the plan for a new caravan straight away and keep the savings as cash, about five months' worth. I'd look at whether I could draw some super early, and I'd ask our son, who's an engineer, if we could lean on him while I find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the night they announced the warehouse robots, but worse, because I'm older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take a payout early. Why early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because last time the first people to go got the best deal. The ones who hung on got less, and some got nothing when the company changed hands. I'd rather go with something in my pocket than wait to be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually look for after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have no idea, honestly. If robots can do hands-on work, I don't know what a fifty-nine-year-old truck driver does. Maybe help my brother-in-law with his rental units. I'm not going to pretend I know.

S2.say: I'd say companies and government both need to slow down and look after people, because two years is too fast for anyone. He'd raise it with his local member if asked.
S2.think: He thinks his mine job would be gone within a year, as full AGI would fix the problems he logged in his notebook. His quarry backup would go the same way.
S2.do: Takes an early payout before the money runs out, drops the caravan plan and holds about five months of savings in cash. Looks at drawing some pension early and asks his engineer son for support while he looks for work.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the night the warehouse robots were announced, but worse because he's older.
S2.quote: I'd rather go with something in my pocket than wait to be pushed.
S2.fieldNote: He applies his warehouse lesson directly: go early, get the better deal. He's honest that he has no idea what work would be left. His centre outlook shows in spreading responsibility between companies and government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so let's plan. The company should tell people what's happening and give real notice. I'd say that at work and leave the arguing to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three. If I play it smart, I could ride a few years in the control room or as one of the guys who looks after the robot trucks, then retire. It's not a disaster, as long as I move at the right moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the control room training as soon as a few others had made it work, probably within the first year. I'd save hard, aiming for a year's worth by 2030, and pay down the car. And I'd keep the notebook going, so I know when the robot trucks are really ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I've got time to be smart about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does "the right moment" look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the robot trucks stop needing guys with rags, the drivers are done within a year. I'd want to be in the control room before that day, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd give up to make this work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fishing trip with my brothers every winter, maybe. And the caravan, again. Elena would say we've given up the caravan in every one of these pictures, and she'd be right.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so let's plan, with the company giving real notice. He'd say it at work and leave the arguing to others.
S3.think: At sixty-three by 2031, he thinks he could spend a few years in the control room or looking after the robot trucks, then retire. It's not a disaster if he moves at the right moment.
S3.do: Joins control room training within the first year once others have made it work. Saves towards a year's cushion by 2030, pays down the car and keeps his notebook to track when the robot trucks are truly ready.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with time to be smart about it.
S3.quote: When the robot trucks stop needing guys with rags, the drivers are done within a year.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets him use his careful, watch-then-move style. His notebook becomes a kind of early warning system. The running joke about the caravan showed his warmth and his realism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and most of us here will be fine if we're sensible. I'd tell the younger drivers to start looking at the control room and maintenance now. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly fine. I'd be sixty-eight, and I'd planned to stop at sixty-five. The only risk is the south pit going driverless before then, which it might anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and get onto the big trucks. If the company opens control room training, I'd take it once it's proven. I'd keep saving the same and help my nephew, who's eighteen, think about which trade lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your nephew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, don't learn to drive the truck, learn to fix the robot. Or better, learn the electrics. I'd show him the north pit from the lookout and say, that's your future, son, so get on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the south pit might go driverless anyway. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But that's the steady one, not this. With ten years and AGI at the end, I think they'd start in the middle somewhere. I'd likely be close enough to sixty-five that a payout would cover the gap.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and most people will be fine if they're sensible. He'd tell younger drivers to look at control room and maintenance work now.
S4.think: He'd be sixty-eight and planned to stop at sixty-five, so it's mostly fine for him. The only risk is the south pit going driverless earlier.
S4.do: Keeps driving and moves to the big trucks, taking control room training once it's proven. Keeps saving as he is and helps his eighteen-year-old nephew pick a lasting trade.
S4.quote: I'd show him the north pit from the lookout and say, that's your future, son, so get on the right side of it.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, David relaxes and turns into a mentor for his nephew. He reasons that by the time any cuts reached him, a payout would cover the gap to sixty-five. His steady, evidence-first habit stays the same throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be out at fifty-nine with no idea what comes next. What would help is a fair payout based on age, not just years served, and being able to draw my super a few years early without a penalty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how many times one person can start over. I've done it once at fifty-five. I'd do it again if I had to, but I'd want someone to tell me the truth early this time, not in the last week.

headlineQuote: I'd want someone to tell me the truth early this time, not in the last week.
portrait: David Diaz is a fifty-eight-year-old former warehouse forklift driver who now drives a haul truck by hand at a gold mine where twelve self-driving trucks already run on the next pit. Having lost his warehouse job to robots, he keeps a notebook comparing the robot trucks with human drivers, and he waits for proof before he moves. He's calm if AI plateaus, anxious with steady change because he's seen it before, and alarmed by AGI in two years, when he'd take an early payout. With five or ten years he plans a timed move into the control room and eases towards retirement at sixty-five.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries him most, because he'd be out of work at fifty-nine with no idea what comes next.
whatWouldHelp: A fair payout based on age rather than just years served, and the ability to draw his pension early without a penalty.
